title: What Is Love Bombing? Signs, Examples and What to Do — cv.cm
description: What is love bombing? Learn the signs, how it differs from real early feelings, example messages, how to slow things down, and when it becomes control.
answer: Love bombing is a pattern where someone floods you with attention, praise, gifts and fast promises early on, then uses the closeness to gain control. Real early feelings can also be intense, but they respect your pace and your "no" and stay consistent over time. If slowing down makes the person angry, cold or guilt-tripping, treat it as a warning sign.

body: Love bombing is not a clinical diagnosis. It is a name for a pattern that support services and researchers see again and again, often at the start of unhealthy or abusive relationships. The intensity is the point: it makes you feel chosen and special very quickly, before you know the person well.

ul: Extreme flattery early on, such as "You are perfect. My life was nothing before you."
Calling you a soulmate or saying "I love you" within days or a few weeks.
Constant messages and calls, with upset or anger when you do not reply fast.
Expensive gifts or offers of money that make you feel you owe something.
Pushing for big steps fast: being exclusive, moving in, meeting family, talking about marriage or children.
Wanting all your free time, and showing irritation when you see friends or family.
Ignoring small boundaries, like showing up when you said you were busy.

body: Any one of these on its own can happen in a normal crush. The pattern matters: many of them together, very fast, and a negative reaction when you set the pace.

sections.h: The cycle: why the attention does not last
body: Domestic abuse services often describe love bombing as the first phase of a cycle. First comes idealization: you are put on a pedestal. Then comes devaluation: criticism, coldness, jealousy or blame start to appear, often after you feel committed. Some relationships then move to discard, where the person pulls away or ends it, sometimes only to return with a new wave of affection.

The cycle works because the early phase sets a very high reference point. When the warmth disappears, many people try harder to win it back, and they blame themselves for the change. The person doing it may then give warmth again for a short time, which keeps the hope alive.

Research on love bombing is still young. A 2017 survey of 484 young adults by Strutzenberg and colleagues, described by the authors as one of the first empirical studies of the topic, linked love-bombing behavior to narcissistic traits and to insecure attachment, and to heavier texting in the relationship. That does not mean every intense partner is a narcissist. It means intense early pursuit can be a strategy to gain power, not only a sign of strong feelings.

sections.h: Love bombing vs genuine early enthusiasm
body: People in love do get excited. Both can feel fast. The difference shows over weeks, and especially when you slow down or say no.

body.note: A simple test: notice what happens the first time you say "not yet". A person with healthy feelings may be a little disappointed. A person who is love bombing usually reacts with pressure, guilt or anger.

sections.h: Example messages and what they may signal
body: Words alone prove nothing. Read messages in context and over time. These examples show the kind of pressure that often appears.

Gifts turned into debt
"I gave that because I wanted to. You don't owe me."

sections.h: How to slow things down and test it
body: You do not have to accuse anyone to protect yourself. Set your own pace and watch the response.

ol: Say your pace clearly and kindly: "I like you, and I want to take this slower. Can we see each other once a week for now?"
Keep your normal life: friends, family, work, hobbies and sleep. Do not cancel plans to fit their schedule.
Reply to messages at your normal speed. You do not need to explain every gap.
Turn down large gifts or money for now: "That's very generous, but I'm not comfortable with gifts like that this early."
Delay big steps such as moving in, joint finances or meeting their family until you have known each other for months, not weeks.
Talk to one trusted friend about how things are going. People outside the relationship often notice pressure first.
Watch for the next few weeks. Look for respect, steadiness and kindness when you say no, not for more grand gestures.

body: If the person accepts your pace and stays warm, that is a good sign. If they become angry, sulk, threaten to leave, or say you are "playing games", you have learned something important. Being honest about your pace is not a game. For a wider list of warning signs, see the red flags article on this shelf.

sections.h: When love bombing is part of coercive control
body: Love bombing becomes part of abuse when the closeness is used to control you. Coercive control is a pattern of behavior that limits your freedom and makes you afraid or dependent. Signs that the pattern has crossed that line include:

ul: Checking your phone, location or messages, or demanding your passwords.
Cutting you off from friends or family, or making contact with them difficult.
Controlling your money, clothes, food, work or where you go.
Threats, including threats to hurt themselves if you leave.
Anger that makes you afraid, or any physical violence or sexual pressure.

body: If this sounds familiar, it is not your fault. Love bombing is designed to feel good, and smart, careful people fall for it. Leaving can feel confusing because you remember the good start. Planning with a support service can make leaving safer.
You can talk to someone even if you are not sure whether it is abuse. Support lines listen and help you think, without pressure to leave before you are ready.

body.note: If you are in danger now, contact your local emergency number. In the US, loveisrespect.org (for dating relationships) and thehotline.org are free and confidential; in other countries, contact a domestic-violence helpline or a local service where you live. If you feel unsafe or think about hurting yourself, contact a crisis line or emergency services.

faq.q: How long does love bombing last?
faq.a: There is no fixed length. It is often weeks to a few months, and it usually changes once you feel committed or once you push back. Some people repeat short bursts of affection after conflict.

faq.q: Can love bombing happen in same-sex relationships or friendships?
faq.a: Yes. Love bombing can happen in any relationship, between people of any gender, and even in friendships or groups. The pattern is the same: fast, intense attention used to create dependence.
Not always. Some people rush because of their own anxiety or because they confuse intensity with love. What matters for you is the effect: whether they respect your pace and your "no".

faq.q: Can I be love bombed over text only?
faq.a: Yes. Constant messages, fast declarations and pressure to talk all day can happen entirely on chat apps, including with someone you have never met. Be careful if fast affection is followed by requests for money.

faq.q: Should I tell the person I think they are love bombing me?
faq.a: You can, but you do not have to. It is often more useful to set your pace and watch the response. If you feel unsafe, focus on your own safety plan rather than a confrontation.
